unresolvedReferences.description: 吾丘子 (Wuqiu Zi) is an allusion; identification with the 丘吾子 of Kongzi jiayu/Shuoyuan (a contemporary of Confucius) is external and uncertain, so his setting is recorded with uncertain certainty.
安偉 (An Wei): the Zhonghua collation notes the passage is corrupt; 安偉 may be an attendant's name or an exclamation, so no person record was created and the en candidates are marked ambiguous.
子義綱: the parallel Zhou shu lists Fan Shen's work 《義綱略論》, so 'son Yigang' may be a textual corruption; recorded as a person of uncertain historicity.
天平二年 conflicts with Fan Shen's Northern Zhou career; the Zhou shu reads 天和二年 (567), used with textual-variant certainty.
The tabooed characters 雄 and 安 presumably refer to the fathers of Xu Zhicai and He Shikai, who are not named as persons in the text; no person records created.
Xu Zunming is listed as a fellow commandery man and co-founding master, but he was Xiong Ansheng's teacher from Huayin; the collation suspects missing text.
The crown prince in the office title 皇太子諫議 is not named; by date (after 570) he would be Yuwen Yun, but this is not stated, so no person link was made.
The emperor issuing the Wucheng 1 edict (Emperor Ming of Zhou) is not named in the text; no person record created.
The emperor addressed as 陛下 in the Baoding 3 memorials is not named; by date he is Emperor Wu of Zhou (r. 560-578), linked with strongly-inferred certainty via role/claims.
許氏 (the Xu school) is read as the tradition of Xu Shen (Shuowen jiezi); the text names only the surname.
文帝 is identified as Emperor Wen of Zhou (Yuwen Tai) on the basis of the parallel Zhou shu (太祖); it could otherwise be read as Emperor Wen of Western Wei.
鐘、王 read as Zhong You and Wang Xizhi (calligraphic exemplars); the text gives only surnames.
The Wei emperor to whom the eleven-year-old Zhao Wenshen presented a writing is not named.
The emperor who accepted Li Jingxi's memorial is unnamed; by date (563-567) Emperor Wu of Zhou.
細腳胡 (father of He Tuo) is rendered 'a Sogdian merchant'; it may be a nickname or name ('Slender-legged Hu') rather than a description. Recorded as an uncertain nickname.
The Prince of Xiangdong is not named; he is presumably Xiao Yi (later Emperor Yuan of Liang).
The emperor who ordered the Xin-Shen debate is unnamed; read as Emperor Wen of Sui from context (strongly inferred).
惟帝難之 quotes the Documents about the ancient emperor (Yao); not linked to a person.
The Jin ruler is unnamed (traditionally Duke Ping of Jin).
